Embodied AI Governance Corpus

← Project hub: all deliverables of the study · current explorer (v5) · this is an earlier version (v2, round 1 only), kept for the record

Embodied AI means AI in a body: robots, self-driving vehicles, drones, surgical and factory machines. This explorer holds 1,656 documents collected by eight regional teams (laws, bills, strategies, standards, guidelines, government reports, research papers and news), each labelled by an AI model against a fixed codebook and checked against a second model on a sample. No human read every document; treat labels as consistent, not certified.

The story in one line: robots are studied far more than they are regulated. The few binding rules that reach them come from vehicle, aviation, workplace and medical-device law or from voluntary ISO standards, and the robots people live with (companions, carers, humanoids) have almost none.

Columns:
What the labels mean (glossary)
Embodied AI, physical AI
AI that controls a machine with a body: robots, self-driving vehicles, drones, surgical and factory machines, as opposed to AI that only produces text, images or decisions on a screen.
About robots or embodied AI
Documents the model rated at least moderately relevant to governing embodied AI, or that name a specific robot type. This is the "embodied-AI set" used in the report (675 documents).
Rules and policies
Governance instruments: laws, regulations, decrees, bills, strategies, guidelines, codes of conduct, standards and resolutions. Research papers and news are not instruments.
Binding law
A statute, regulation, decree or order whose breach has legal consequences. "Voluntary guidance" (soft law) and technical standards cannot be enforced on their own, though laws often point to standards.
Technical standard
A detailed voluntary engineering specification (for example ISO 10218 for factory robots, ISO 13482 for care robots) that says how to make a machine safe.
Status
Where an instrument is in its life: proposal, bill under consideration, consultation open, adopted but not yet in force, in force, published and current, superseded or repealed.
In depth vs in passing
A principle is "in depth" when the document says what must be done, by whom and how it is checked; "in passing" when it is only named.
Relevance
The model's 0 to 3 rating of how central embodied-AI governance is to the document (3 = the document is about it).
Confidence
The model's own 0 to 1 confidence in its labels; lower for partial captures and landing pages.
Excluded captures
Files that were bot-walls, empty pages, wrong documents or off-topic; hidden by default and listed when the box is ticked.
How the data were made, and what to be careful about

Eight regional teams collected sources in two exercises: a sprint for robot-specific material and a database of general AI-governance instruments. Files were converted to text, duplicates merged, and every document was labelled by Claude Sonnet 5.5 under a fixed codebook (39 fields). A second model (Claude Opus 5.5) re-labelled a 10% sample (median agreement kappa 0.89); the main model was re-run on the same sample (0.95) and on the full text instead of an excerpt (0.84). Keyword searches over the full text were used as an independent check. Years are the dates stated in the documents, inferred from content where unstated.

Generated 2026-10-30 from data/master_table.csv (1,656 captured documents; 1,538 usable). Figure data and tables are in the project package.

Be careful with: Europe is 44% of the usable documents and English 78%; Chinese-language documents are essentially absent; the collection sought research on robots and official texts on AI in general, so the ratio of research to rules is partly by design; counts of instruments are lower bounds (the collection is not a census); 2026 runs to October; percentages over small groups (fewer than 30 documents) are shown as counts.

Region follows the issuing jurisdiction or first author's affiliation, so it can differ from the folder a document was collected under. "Year" is the annotated publication or adoption date, falling back to OpenAlex for DOI-matched papers and then to PDF metadata. Summaries in the record panel were written by the AI model from the document text.
